newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines' trade deficit hits record $10.09 bln.
newsitem.headline: Philippines' trade deficit hits record $10.09 bln.

text.p: The Philippines' trade deficit widened to a record $10.09 billion in the first 10 months of the year, but economists said inflows of overseas earnings would help offset the disadvantages of the trade shortfall.

The National Statistics Office reported on Friday that the merchandise trade deficit ballooned by 41.2 percent to an all-time high of $10.09 billion as of October this year from $7.148 billion posted in same period last year.
Imports grew 24.81 percent while exports grew 16.70 percent.

"The deficit is still manageable over the next two or three years, so long as the overseas contract workers maintain their pace," Josef Yap, a fellow at government think-tank Philippine Institute for Development Studies (PIDS), told Reuters.
Filipinos working overseas are a major source of foreign exchange for the country with their remittances accounting for $3.4 billion in the first six months of the year.
Increased interest in the Philippines following the launch of economic reforms have also led to higher foreign investments in the stock market as well as direct investments.
The inflows had boosted the country's gross national product (GNP) to 7.1 percent in the first nine months of the year compared to 5.3 percent in the year-ago period.
"Overseas workers are the major exports of the Philippines," said Manuel Goseco, chief economist at Dharmala Securities.
PIDS' Yap said the higher foreign portfolio investments would likewise cover the payment for merchandise imports.
The Central Bank has beefed up its foreign exchange reserves to $11.6 billion as of November 20.
Goseco said growing import bills were necessary for a growing economy.
"The acceleration of imports is a necessary evil for the expansion of the country's industrial base," he said, adding that a majority of the imports were capital goods and raw materials.
The government is projecting a $12 billion trade deficit by the end of the year.

But Yap said the government must solve the country's low savings rate, which had led to dependence on foreign investments and loans that might dry up in the coming years as more lucrative markets emerge.
Other economists were not as sanguine about the growing trade deficit.

"A wide trade deficit is often attributed to high imports, but the situation has another side worth noting: a trade deficit occurs primarily because of weak exports," said Richard Supangan, an economist at the University of Asia & Pacific.
He blamed the slower export growth to the relatively stronger peso.

Recent calls by some exporters to let the peso weaken were firmly rejected by the Central Bank, which said the rate of about 26.26 pesos to the U.S. dollar was determined by the market and the bank acted only to reduce sharp fluctuations.

Supangan said another cause for concern was the country's limited range of exports, which made it susceptible to downturns in those industries. A majority of the country's exports are electronic components and textiles.

"This is something that the government has to look into. It's not a big concern right now, but it is something that will be always there at the back of our mind," said Spencer Yap, an analyst at BPI Securities.
